pluss::timeline::arange¶

Back to Timeline Factory API Reference

Signatures¶

Timeline pluss::timeline::arange(const Timeline& start,
                                 const Timeline& end,
                                 const Duration& step,
                                 bool inclusive = true)
Timeline pluss::timeline::arange(std::string_view start,
                                 std::string_view end,
                                 const Duration& step,
                                 bool inclusive = true)
Timeline pluss::timeline::arange(std::string_view start,
                                 std::string_view end,
                                 std::int64_t step = 1,
                                 bool inclusive = true)

Build A Sequence From An Exact Step¶

arange() begins at start, repeatedly adds one scalar Duration, and returns the generated instants as a rank-one Timeline. It is the appropriate range factory when the interval is already known as elapsed nanoseconds, seconds, hours, or another exact duration. Use date_range() instead when a named calendar frequency, especially a local calendar day, is the intended rule.

The Timeline overload accepts any two scalar instants. The text overload with a Duration accepts matching date-only, time-only, or complete timestamp text. The integer overload is deliberately narrower: an integer means elapsed days for date-only text and elapsed seconds for time-only text. Complete timestamps must use an explicit Duration, preventing a bare integer from acquiring a surprising unit.

inclusive=true includes end only when repeated stepping lands on it. inclusive=false always excludes end. Neither setting inserts an off-grid endpoint. A positive step advances toward a later endpoint; a negative step advances toward an earlier endpoint. A sign pointing away from the endpoint produces an empty vector rather than reversing the sign.

Every step is elapsed time. A 24-hour Duration is always 86,400 seconds; it is not a promise to preserve a displayed local clock through an offset change. The result retains start.tz(), while end is used only as an instant boundary.

Example 1: Timeline Endpoints And An Open Boundary¶

const auto ticks = pluss::timeline::arange(
    pluss::timeline::from_epoch(0LL),
    pluss::timeline::from_epoch(7LL),
    pluss::duration::nanos(2),
    false);
std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::timeline::format(ticks, "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000000+00:00", "1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000002+00:00", "1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000004+00:00", "1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000006+00:00"]

The exact two-nanosecond interval is retained. Seven nanoseconds is off-grid, so changing inclusive to true would not append it.

Example 2: Date Text Gives Integer Steps A Day Unit¶

const auto days = pluss::timeline::arange(
    "2024-02-27", "2024-03-02", 2);
std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::timeline::format(days, "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["2024-02-27T00:00:00.000000000+00:00", "2024-02-29T00:00:00.000000000+00:00", "2024-03-02T00:00:00.000000000+00:00"]

The sequence crosses leap day without special casing because each integer step means an exact 24-hour duration from a UTC date anchor.

Example 3: Time Text Gives Integer Steps A Second Unit¶

const auto seconds = pluss::timeline::arange(
    "09:30:00", "09:30:03", 1, false);
std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::timeline::format(seconds, "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["1970-01-01T09:30:00.000000000+00:00", "1970-01-01T09:30:01.000000000+00:00", "1970-01-01T09:30:02.000000000+00:00"]

Clock-only text is anchored to 1970-01-01 UTC, just as it is for time().

Example 4: Descending Sequences¶

const auto descending = pluss::timeline::arange(
    "2024-03-03", "2024-02-28", -2);
std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::timeline::format(descending, "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["2024-03-03T00:00:00.000000000+00:00", "2024-03-01T00:00:00.000000000+00:00", "2024-02-28T00:00:00.000000000+00:00"]

Example 5: A Direction Mismatch Is Empty¶

const auto empty = pluss::timeline::arange(
    "2024-03-03", "2024-02-28", 2);
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(empty) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[0], tz=UTC)[  ]

The result is a defined rank-one value with zero elements.

Example 6: Exact Hours Across An Offset Transition¶

const auto first = pluss::timeline::make("2024-03-10T05:00:00Z")
                       .tz_convert("America/New_York");
const auto last = pluss::timeline::make("2024-03-10T08:00:00Z")
                      .tz_convert("America/New_York");
const auto hours = pluss::timeline::arange(
    first, last, pluss::duration::hours(1));

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::timeline::format(hours, "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["2024-03-10T00:00:00.000000000-05:00", "2024-03-10T01:00:00.000000000-05:00", "2024-03-10T03:00:00.000000000-04:00", "2024-03-10T04:00:00.000000000-04:00"]

Adjacent instants remain one elapsed hour apart. The local clock skips 02:00 because that wall time does not exist during this transition.

Validation And Failure¶

All three object arguments must be scalar. Endpoints and the step must be defined, and the step must be nonzero. Text endpoints must have the same kind; date text cannot be paired with clock text. Complete timestamp text rejects an integer step. Generation stops safely before integer addition would overflow.

try {
  const auto start = pluss::timeline::date("2024-01-01");
  const auto end = pluss::timeline::date("2024-01-03");
  (void)pluss::timeline::arange(
      start, end, pluss::duration::nanos(pluss::Duration::kNaT));
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "rejected\n";
}

Output¶

rejected
